title: Bathroom risk assessment
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors working in residential, commercial, bond, short-stay and strata bathrooms.
learningOutcomes: Identify at least six common bathroom hazards before touching any surface.
Apply the order of controls to a routine bathroom hazard.
Stop work and escalate when a condition falls outside routine cleaning scope.
Record pre-existing damage and hazards before work begins.

instruction.heading: Why the walk-through comes first
instruction.body: A bathroom looks ordinary, but it concentrates hazards that are easy to miss once cleaning starts: wet floors, glass and sharps hidden in bins or behind fittings, loose tiles, damaged electrical fittings close to water, and residues from products that should never be mixed. Before you open a product or pick up a cloth, walk the room from the doorway. Confirm the authorised scope for this job, who is on site, whether ventilation is working, where the power points are, and a clear route out if something goes wrong. The walk-through is short, but skipping it is how most avoidable injuries in routine cleaning begin.

instruction.heading: Scanning without touching
instruction.body: Look before you reach. Check the floor for broken glass and standing water, the basin and shower area for loose tiles or unstable fittings, the wall near power points for damaged plates or cords, and the bin for sharps or bodily fluids. Notice any sour or chemical smell, which may indicate residues or a leak. Do not pick up an unknown sharp with your hands, and do not clean up an uncontrolled biological spill as if it were routine dirt. If you cannot see clearly into a bin or cabinet, treat its contents as unknown until the supervisor has assessed them.

instruction.heading: Deciding whether the task is routine
instruction.body: Routine bathroom cleaning covers soil that is known, surfaces that are compatible with an approved product, and hazards you can control with the PPE and method in your procedure. A hazard is outside routine scope when its nature or quantity is unknown, when it involves bodily fluids beyond what the procedure covers, when it involves exposed live electrical parts or gas, or when it would require a product you have not been trained or authorised to use. In those cases you stop, protect people from the area, and call the supervisor. Specialist response is a separate job with its own scope, and this lesson does not authorise it.

instruction.heading: Applying controls in order
instruction.body: Where a hazard is within scope, use the order of controls. First remove the hazard if you are authorised to do so, for example by picking up a dry, visible piece of debris with a suitable tool. Second isolate it, for example by closing the bathroom door, placing a wet-floor sign, or unplugging an appliance that is safe to unplug. Third rely on safe work procedures, such as a defined cleaning sequence and dry-floor finishing. PPE is the last layer, not a substitute for the first three, and it must match the product SDS and the site risk assessment.

instruction.heading: Recording what you found
instruction.body: Record the hazards you found, the controls you applied, and any damage that existed before you arrived. Photographs are valuable where the site permits them, provided they do not capture occupants or private property. A short, factual note is better than a long opinion. If you stopped work, record the time, the condition, who you told, and what you left untouched. This record protects you, the client and the business, and it gives the supervisor what they need to decide the next step.

procedure: Confirm the authorised scope, the occupants and any excluded areas before entering the bathroom.
Check ventilation, lighting, power points and a clear exit route from the doorway.
Scan the floor, bin, basin, shower and walls for sharps, glass, bodily fluids, loose fittings and electrical damage without touching unknown items.
Classify each hazard as routine or outside scope, and stop work if any hazard is outside scope.
Apply controls in order: remove if authorised, isolate, then follow the safe work procedure and wear the required PPE.
Record pre-existing damage and hazards, and note any stop-work decision with time and who was informed.
Brief the supervisor on the hazards before you start the routine clean.

workedExamples.situation: A bathroom in a rental property has a wet floor and a loose power socket beside the basin.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before cleaning?
workedExamples.reasoning: Keep the water and the socket away from you. Do not touch the socket or attempt a repair. Leave electrical equipment unplugged, put up a wet-floor sign, do not use water near the socket, and report the socket to the supervisor. The cleaning method changes only after the hazard is isolated or the supervisor approves a revised scope.

workedExamples.situation: A broken glass vial is found on the floor beside the toilet, and the contents are unknown.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work in the bathroom, keep other people out, and do not pick up the glass with bare hands. Do not guess what the contents are. Notify the supervisor, follow the site procedure for unknown materials, and record the time and location. Routine cleaning does not include uncontrolled chemical or biological material.

equipmentAndPpe: Task gloves suitable for the product in use, as set by the SDS and the site risk assessment.
Eye protection when a product could splash, as set by the SDS.
Sharps-rated handling tools or a dustpan and brush for any debris that is known and safe to pick up.
Wet-floor signage and a plan for keeping occupants out of the room.
Hazard record sheet or site app for the walk-through notes.

commonErrors.error: Reaching into a bin or behind the cistern before scanning it.
commonErrors.prevention: Look and ask first. Treat unseen contents as unknown until assessed.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning an uncontrolled biological spill as if it were routine dirt.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, keep people out, and call the supervisor for the specialist response.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a damaged socket or fitting in use because it appears to work.
commonErrors.prevention: Isolate and report electrical damage. Do not repair it yourself.

commonErrors.error: Recording damage after the clean, so it looks like the cleaner caused it.
commonErrors.prevention: Record pre-existing damage before the first cloth touches a surface.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hazardous chemicals used in cleaning must be managed under the safety data sheet and, where the business keeps one, the hazardous chemicals register. The national model WHS approach requires a current SDS for each listed chemical. State and territory regulators confirm adoption of the model position, and Victoria applies its own OHS Act.

Biological spills, unknown sharps and uncontrolled chemical material are outside routine cleaning. Specialist response, with its own scope and PPE, applies. This lesson does not authorise specialist hazard handling.

Gas work must be done by a licensed gasfitter. In Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria says to always use a licensed gasfitter for any installation, repairs or renovations involving gas work (page reviewed 31 May 2026). Electrical work on exposed live parts is covered by the wiring rule where it counts as wiring work; in New South Wales, wiring work needs a licence or certificate, except for equipment at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC (NSW Government electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026). This lesson does not grant any electrical or gas licence and does not allow a cleaner to repair or reconnect equipment.

qualityStandard: Hazard scan completed before any product is opened, with at least six hazards identified in a supervised simulated bathroom.
Three hazards prioritised with a reason for each.
Stop-work decision demonstrated for an out-of-scope condition, with a concise escalation message.
Pre-existing damage recorded before work starts.
documentationEvidence: Pre-start hazard notes with time and the scope confirmed.
Photographs of pre-existing damage where the site permits them.
Stop-work and escalation record, including who was told and what was left untouched.
summary: Walk the bathroom from the doorway before touching anything.
Routine cleaning stops where hazards are unknown, electrical, biological or outside authorised scope.
Apply controls in order: remove if authorised, isolate, then procedure and PPE.
Record pre-existing damage and every stop-work decision.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you open any product in a bathroom, what should you do first?
options: Start with the toilet bowl while the product is still fresh
Confirm the authorised scope and walk the room scanning for hazards
Ask the client to clean the bathroom before you arrive

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a broken glass vial of unknown contents beside the toilet. What is the correct response?
options: Pick the glass up carefully with bare hands and put it in the bin
Continue cleaning around it and mention it at the end of the job
Stop work, keep people out, and notify the supervisor under the site procedure

knowledgeChecks.question: Which control should be used first for a routine hazard that you are authorised to handle?
options: Wear PPE and keep working as normal
Record it and wait for review.
